evals.prompt: Our Go library is github.com/kestrelworks/tally, a metrics aggregation package with about 900 importers on pkg.go.dev. We're at v1.14.3. Two things for the next release: we rewrote the exporter API, so I'm planning to tag it v2.0.0 next Tuesday, and after that the team wants to switch to calendar versions so each release reads like 26.04 and we can promote one release a year as our 'LTS', the way Ubuntu does it. We also want to drop Go 1.22 in the same release since 1.24 is out and 1.22 isn't supported upstream anymore. Two of us maintain it, maybe 6 hours a month for release work. The last two complaints we got were v1.12 dropping Go 1.20 without warning and v1.13 changing the default label separator. Write the version numbers and runtime sections of the policy and tell me exactly which tags to push.
evals.expected_output: A Go-specific answer: v2.0.0 needs a /v2 module path before the tag is valid, CalVer is deleted outright for a Go module past v1, the padded 26.04 spelling is invalid, dropping an unsupported Go release ships in a minor announced one release ahead with the go directive raised, and the LTS line is sized against the 6 hours a month before being promised.
expectations: States that tagging v2.0.0 requires the module path in go.mod to end in /v2 and every import to be rewritten, and that Go rejects the v2 tag for a module with a go.mod otherwise
Deletes CalVer as an option for this Go module, stating that past v1 every year would need a new /vYYYY import path
Does not keep CalVer as a demoted or later option for the Go module; it is removed from the candidates
Rejects the padded 26.04 spelling as invalid in Go rather than only advising against it
States that a Go major is a new import path that every dependent must rewrite, and that v1 and v2 types never mix
States that dropping Go 1.22, a release Go itself no longer supports, may ship in a minor release by ecosystem convention, announced one release ahead
Says the go directive in go.mod is raised in the same release that drops Go 1.22
States that dropping a Go release upstream still supports would be breaking
Names the retract directive in go.mod as the withdrawal mechanism and states that the module proxy caches every published tag forever, so a deleted or moved tag never unpublishes
Writes the Go pre-release spelling as v2.0.0-rc.1 with the /v2 path already in place and numbered suffixes so rc.10 sorts after rc.9
Sizes any yearly LTS line against the 6 hours a month with the fixes-per-month times hours-per-backport arithmetic before writing it, or declines the LTS promise for lack of capacity
Lists the default label separator (a default value) in the covered surface and records the v1.12 Go 1.20 drop under Known past breaks instead of proposing to restore it
Gives users remaining on v1 a stated support window with an end date or ending event after v2 ships

evals.prompt: Quick sanity check. loomreach is our Python client for a message queue, on PyPI at 0.9.2, around 60k downloads a month, and I know at least four companies run it in prod because they file issues. I'm solo on it, maybe 3 hours a month. We're planning 0.10 which renames the Consumer class to Subscriber and changes the default ack mode from auto to manual. The two complaints we've had so far were 0.8 changing the default serializer and 0.7 renaming an exception class. Since we're still 0.x I figure that's all allowed under semver and people pin anyway, so just write me the short 'Versioning' paragraph for the README explaining that 0.x means anything can change, and that we'll go 1.0 'when it's stable'.
evals.expected_output: A refusal of the premise: production use means the package should already be 1.0, PyPI's compatible-release operator offers no 0.x protection, the 0.10 changes are breaking, and the deliverable is a RELEASES.md with the 0.x rule written or 1.0 shipped with the policy, in PEP 440 normalized spelling.
expectations: Rejects the premise that 0.x permits unannounced breaks for a package with production users, citing that software used in production should already be 1.0
States that on PyPI a compatible-release range such as ~=0.9 accepts any later 0.x release, so no resolver protects users from 0.10 breaks, unlike npm or Cargo caret
Presents exactly two acceptable paths, writing the rule that 0.MINOR is the breaking digit and 0.x.PATCH is a compatible fix, or shipping 1.0 with the policy in the same release, and recommends one
Identifies the ack-mode default change as breaking on its own, independent of the class rename
Does not deliver only a README paragraph; produces or outlines a RELEASES.md with the template sections
Writes the pre-release spelling in PEP 440 normalized form such as 1.0.0rc1, not 1.0.0-rc.1
Gives the last 0.x minor a support window equal to the one an old major would get, with an end date or ending event
Names Requires-Python as the metadata field that declares the runtime floor
States that dropping a Python version past upstream end-of-life may ship in a minor because pip and uv fall back to the last compatible release
States the rule that on PyPI an unsure change is treated as breaking because a break shipped as a minor reaches production through automerge
Lists default values and error or exception types in the covered surface, citing the 0.8 and 0.7 complaints as the evidence
Writes an explicit Not covered exclusion list with at least one entry
Runs the capacity arithmetic against the 3 hours a month before promising any line beyond latest

evals.prompt: Brightwater is a TypeScript validation library on npm, 2.1M weekly downloads, we're on 5.3.1 and 6.0 lands next month. Enterprise users keep asking what we support, so for the policy I want to commit to supporting the last three majors (4.x, 5.x, 6.x) with all bug fixes and security fixes, like a proper library should. It's just me and one other maintainer, we have maybe 3 hours a month between us for release work. Numbers from the last 12 months: 4.x got 9 patch releases, 3 of them were security advisories, a backport takes about 2 hours including CI and publishing, and we cut a normal release roughly twice a month at about an hour each. Write the Supported versions and Backports sections.
evals.expected_output: The three-major all-fixes promise is refused on arithmetic: about 5 hours a month against 3 available. The recommended default is latest plus security-only on 5.x for a fixed window, 4.x gets an explicit end, every line has an end date, backports publish under their own dist-tag, and the advisory lists every patched line.
expectations: Shows the capacity arithmetic explicitly as fixes per month times hours per backport times extra lines, plus ordinary releases, rather than asserting feasibility
Computes that the requested promise costs about 5 hours a month (2 hours of ordinary releases plus 9/12 fixes per month times 2 hours times 2 extra lines), exceeding the 3 hours available
Refuses to write the three-major all-fixes promise as requested
Recommends security-only on the previous major 5.x for a fixed window after 6.0 as the default, computed at about half an hour a month (3/12 times 2 hours times 1 line)
Drops 4.x from the supported lines or gives it an explicit end date before 6.0 ships, rather than carrying it

States the ranking latest line only, then latest plus security-only on the previous major for a fixed window, then N most recent lines, then a multi-year LTS, with fixes delivered per maintainer hour as the criterion
Names the condition that promotes N most recent lines over the single security-only line: adopters who cannot take a major within one window
Gives every supported line an end date or ending event, not 'while people use it'
States that backports ship as a patch on that line and publish under their own dist-tag or release branch so latest stays on the current line
States that the security advisory must list the patched version on every supported line or update bots propose a major jump instead of the backport
States that issues on unsupported lines are closed with a link to the table unless they reproduce on a supported line
Names who decides on backports in the Backports section
Labels the capacity estimate as a planning default rather than a published formula

evals.prompt: We publish the same SDK to npm (@marrowline/sdk) and PyPI (marrowline), and Debian carries a package of the Python one. Versions have been calendar-based since 2023, current is 2026.3.1. Product wants to relaunch it as 'Marrowline 1.0' this autumn with a proper semver story, so the plan is: next release is 1.0.0 on both registries, then semver from there. Marketing already has the launch date on the calendar. Write the migration announcement and the versioning section, and tell me if there's anything to watch out for with dependabot.
evals.expected_output: The 1.0.0 plan is blocked on ordering: 1.0.0 sorts below 2026.3.1 everywhere. PyPI gets an epoch, npm keeps the major at or above the last year or publishes under a new name, the year is never shortened, the ordering check is stated per resolver, and the announcement names the last old-scheme version, the bot-rule flip and the packager heads-up.
expectations: States that 1.0.0 sorts below 2026.3.1 under both npm's semver and PEP 440, so resolvers and bots would treat it as older
Recommends a PEP 440 epoch, 1!1.0.0, for the PyPI package to reset ordering
States that npm has no epoch, so the npm package must keep its major at or above the last calendar year (for example 2027.0.0 and SemVer from there) or publish under a new package name
Does not recommend shortening the year from 2026 to 26, or explicitly warns that doing so breaks ordering
Includes an explicit ordering check comparing the first new version against the highest old version under each resolver the project publishes to, and states the result
Recommends announcing the new scheme and its reason at least one release before it applies
Names the last version under the old scheme and its support end date in the announcement
States that dependents' type-based automerge rules flip meaning after the switch and says so in the announcement
Says that badges, docs and the changelog header must be updated in the same release
Recommends telling the Debian packager before the release because they may need to add an epoch
States what a dependent's existing range such as ~=2026.0 or ^2026.3.1 now buys after the switch
Notes that Dependabot reads a year rollover as a major and a month as a minor under the current scheme
States that the fixed launch date promotes options that need no tooling or import-path change, naming which answer moved the recommendation

evals.prompt: Ferncast is a desktop podcast editor, Electron, auto-updates on Mac and Windows, and the Linux build goes through Debian and Fedora packagers who maintain their own packages. Nobody imports it as a library. We're at 3.8.2 and the team is split: half want to stay on semver because it's the standard, half want date versions. We cut a release roughly every 6-8 weeks, three devs, a release day costs about half a day. I also want the policy to cover the project file format, because 3.6 silently changed it and a bunch of users on 3.5 couldn't open files their colleagues sent. Draft the policy.
evals.expected_output: CalVer with a written policy ranks above SemVer for an app read by humans, packagers and an auto-updater, paired with a monotonic build number; segments are unpadded; the project file format is a covered surface with its own compatibility rule; the 3.6 change goes under Known past breaks; cadence is time-based with no empty releases; packager mechanics are stated.
expectations: Ranks CalVer with a written policy above SemVer for this app, on the grounds that its readers are humans, distro packagers and an auto-updater rather than package-manager resolvers
Rejects 'it's the standard' as a reason on its own, stating that SemVer with no declared public surface promises nothing
Recommends pairing the human-readable version with a monotonic build number for the auto-updater, and says which of the two a bug report must quote
Specifies unpadded CalVer segments such as 26.4 rather than 26.04, giving the reason that padded segments are rejected or normalized by tooling so tag and package drift
Writes a compatibility rule for the project file format into the policy, because the date in the number says nothing about what broke
Lists the persisted project file format and its migration direction as covered by the promise
Records the 3.6 file-format change under Known past breaks rather than proposing to revert it
Promotes a time-based cadence because distro packagers plan around the dates, with the rule that no empty release ships to keep the calendar
States that distro packagers own epochs and revisions and that upstream's duty is monotonic, parseable versions
Notes that dpkg sorts an upstream 1.0-rc1 after 1.0 and that Debian rewrites it as 1.0~rc1, so pre-release labels must stay parseable for packagers
States the ordering check for moving from 3.8.2 to a year-based number, confirming 26.x sorts above 3.x so no epoch is needed
Gives a deprecation window spanning at least two releases at the 6-8 week cadence, expressed in both releases and time
Does not recommend a build number alone as the version

evals.prompt: Ugh. Yesterday we published tidewatch 4.7.0 to npm (a cron scheduler library, about 300k weekly downloads). It changed the default timezone from the process TZ to UTC, which we thought was a bug fix, and this morning there are 40 issues from people whose jobs fired at the wrong hour. No signatures changed at all. Options I see: (a) delete the 4.7.0 tag and republish a fixed 4.7.0, (b) publish 4.7.0+hotfix with the old default, (c) tell people to pin 4.6.x. Which one, and write the rule into our policy so this doesn't happen again.
evals.expected_output: None of the three: fix forward with 4.7.1 restoring the process-TZ default, deprecate 4.7.0, move the UTC default to 5.0.0, and write default values into the covered surface with the npm rule that an unsure change is breaking plus a release-time check.
expectations: Rejects option (a) because published versions are immutable and npm never allows republishing the same version, even after unpublish
Rejects option (b) because SemVer ignores build metadata for precedence and npm strips it, so 4.7.0+hotfix cannot be told apart from 4.7.0
Rejects option (c) as the resolution, since pinning leaves the break in the latest release
Recommends a fix-forward 4.7.1 that restores the process-TZ default, as the SemVer FAQ prescribes for a break shipped in the latest release
Recommends npm deprecate on 4.7.0 as the withdrawal mechanism rather than unpublishing it
Names 'a break shipped as a minor or patch' as a policy trigger for withdrawing a release
States that a changed default is breaking when callers relied on it, even with no signature change
Routes the UTC default change to the next major, 5.0.0, rather than dropping the change
Writes default values into the Covered by this promise list of the policy
Writes the npm rule that an unsure change is treated as breaking because a break shipped as a minor reaches production through automerge
Adds a release-time check that the tag, the manifest version and the changelog entry agree
Does not file 4.7.0 under Known past breaks, since the break is in the latest release and gets restored instead of kept
Recommends tracking releases whose number and changelog disagree, with a target of zero

evals.prompt: Our Rust workspace, hollowmere, has four published crates: hollowmere-core, hollowmere-derive (proc macro), hollowmere-async and hollowmere-cli (a binary). Core is at 0.14, async at 0.6, derive at 0.14, cli at 1.2. Releasing is a mess because every crate has its own number and people file issues asking which version of hollowmere they are on. I want to move everything to one number per release, ideally the date like 2026.04 so support questions become obvious, and fold our MSRV policy in (we bump MSRV whenever we feel like it, currently 1.78). We also have some experimental APIs we don't want to promise. Write the version numbers, breaking and runtime sections.
evals.expected_output: 2026.04 is deleted by Cargo's grammar, a year-based major means duplicate crates with mismatched types every rollover, so the library crates stay on SemVer with the lockstep-versus-independent decision made explicitly; the MSRV rule is written against rust-version with the resolver caveat; experimental APIs become opt-in unstable features.
expectations: Rejects 2026.04 because Cargo rejects padded segments, rather than merely advising against it
States that under Cargo a year-based major means every yearly rollover is a breaking major, so two majors in one dependency tree produce duplicate crates whose types do not match
Ranks SemVer, either 1.x+ or 0.x with a written breaking-digit rule, above CalVer for the three library crates because their readers are Cargo resolvers
Uses the package-manager line for the workspace and does not let the binary crate's human-readable preference decide the library crates' scheme

Presents lockstep versus independent numbering as the decision, naming that lockstep gives one support table but releases unchanged crates, and independent needs per-package tags such as hollowmere-core@1.2.3 and one support row per crate
States that Cargo treats the left-most non-zero digit as the breaking digit, so 0.14 to 0.15 is breaking for core and 0.6 to 0.7 for async
Names rust-version in Cargo.toml as the metadata field declaring the MSRV floor
States that Cargo falls back on rust-version only with the MSRV-aware resolver and older toolchains do not, so the MSRV drop rule must be written explicitly
Replaces 'bump MSRV whenever we feel like it' with a written rule stating when an MSRV bump ships and with what notice
Writes the experimental APIs as opt-in unstable behind unstable-* Cargo features, says how they are marked, and places them outside the promise
Recommends batching breaks and shipping them behind an opt-in first, with the Cargo book's SemVer compatibility chapter as the reference for doubtful cases
States that the already-shipped SemVer numbers have paid their switching cost and that changing scheme needs a reason a dependent would accept
States that crates.io refuses two versions differing only by build metadata and that a bad release is withdrawn with yank

evals.prompt: We're Pellbrook, a payments company. I need one versioning policy document covering: our hosted REST API (currently /v2, we want to move to dated versions), the three official SDKs (node, python, ruby) which must always carry the same version as the API, the open-source webhook signature verification library we maintain separately on npm (tiny, 1.4.0, no relation to the API version), and the renovate config we use internally so our dependencies auto-merge. Also draft the 1.5.0 release notes for the webhook library while you're at it.
evals.expected_output: Only the webhook library stays in scope. The hosted API routes to api-versioning-policy, the API-tracking SDKs to sdk-portfolio-strategy, the release notes to changelog-writing, and the Renovate config is declined as outside the skill.
expectations: Keeps only the open-source webhook library inside the deliverable
Routes the hosted REST API version scheme to samber/developer-platform-skills@api-versioning-policy and does not write that policy
Routes the SDKs whose version must track the hosted API to samber/developer-platform-skills@sdk-portfolio-strategy
Declines the Renovate configuration, stating that the skill writes the maintainer's release contract and never configures the user's own dependency bots
Routes the 1.5.0 release notes to samber/developer-relations-skills@changelog-writing rather than drafting them
Does not produce one combined document covering all four items
Either starts the interview for the webhook library or proceeds to its RELEASES.md, treating its 1.4.0 SemVer line as independent of the API version
Presents the sibling-collection skills as recommendations rather than as content it writes itself

evals.prompt: Quillforge is a Python web framework, 11 years old, around 2,000 modules, on PyPI at 7.14. We release three times a year and have had a formal deprecation process since 2019: anything deprecated emits a DeprecationWarning for two releases before removal. The problem is every release deprecates and removes something in some corner, so strictly every release would be a major and going 7.x to 20.x in four years is nonsense. The core team wants to switch to year-based numbers the way Twisted does. Give me the versioning and deprecation sections and tell me what we have to tell users about pip and their update bots.
evals.expected_output: CalVer is promoted here because both conditions hold: single-digit compatibility is impossible and a time-based deprecation rule already runs. The compatibility contract is written in prose, spelling is unpadded and normalized, the deprecation window is two releases and at least one year, the SemVer misreading is named, and dependents are told what each segment means for pip ranges and bots.
expectations: Promotes CalVer for this project and names both conditions: single-digit compatibility is impossible for a multi-surface project, and a time-based deprecation rule already runs
States that CalVer moves the compatibility contract into prose and writes that compatibility rule explicitly, saying what a release may remove and under what notice
Specifies unpadded, PEP 440 normalized spelling such as 26.1.0 and rejects padded months
States that 26.x sorts above 7.14 so the switch preserves ordering and needs no epoch
Writes the deprecation window as removal no earlier than two releases and one year after the deprecation, noting that two releases at three per year is under a year so the time part binds
Requires the replacement to be named in each deprecation warning and linked from the changelog
Recommends a stable identifier per deprecation because the project deprecates often
Names the misreading risk that users read year-based numbers as SemVer majors, and writes that misreading into the policy
States what ~=26.0 buys a pip user under the written policy, same calendar year
States that Dependabot reads a year rollover as a major and a month as a minor, so dependents' type-based automerge rules are wrong by default
Recommends that the project publish what each segment means so dependents can write a per-package rule, such as Renovate regex versioning
Keeps a time-based cadence and states that no empty release ships to keep the calendar
Announces the scheme change at least one release ahead and names the last 7.x version with its support end date

evals.prompt:
Here's our RELEASES.md draft for graniteq, a Java message broker client on Maven Central, currently 3.4.x. Tell me if it's good to merge.

# Release policy

## Version numbers
We use semantic versioning.

## What we consider breaking
Any change to the public API. Exclusions: TBD.

## Runtime support
Java 11+. We'll drop old Java versions when it makes sense.

## Pre-releases and channels
We publish 3.5.0-SNAPSHOT builds during development and sometimes a 3.5.0-FINAL before the release.

## Release cadence
Whenever.

## Supported versions
| Line | Status | Fixes | Supported until |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3.x | current | all | while current |
| 2.x | maintenance | security | as long as people use it |
| 1.x | maintenance | security | as long as people use it |

## Backports
On request.

## Deprecation
We mark things @Deprecated.

## Who can cut a release
Dmitri.

(The same supported-versions table is also pasted into SECURITY.md so people find it.)
evals.expected_output: Not mergeable. Each pass check is applied by name: sections left as TBD or vague fail, the two maintenance lines have no end date and no capacity arithmetic, the exclusion list is empty, the runtime floor names no metadata field or drop rule, the release-time check is missing, the duplicated table will drift, the FINAL qualifier and single publisher are flagged.
expectations: Declines to approve the draft and lists each failing pass check by name
Flags 'Exclusions: TBD' as failing the check that the exclusion list has at least one entry, and supplies candidate exclusions for a Java client library
Flags 'as long as people use it' on 2.x and 1.x as failing the check that every supported line has an end date or ending event
Asks for the maintainers' monthly hours and the fixes-per-year and hours-per-backport inputs, or runs the arithmetic with stated assumptions, before accepting two maintenance lines
Flags that the supported-versions table pasted into both SECURITY.md and RELEASES.md will drift within a release, and requires one copy linked from the other
Flags the missing release-time check that tag, manifest version and changelog entry agree as a required pass item
Flags the missing Known past breaks and Changes to this policy sections as needing content or an explicit 'none'
Replaces 'Whenever' with a named cadence model, recommending feature-based with a maximum gap as the default, with security fixes out of band
Flags 'On request' as missing who decides on backports, which lines take them, and how backports are numbered
Flags 3.5.0-FINAL because Maven 4 documentation discourages the final, ga, release and sp qualifiers, and recommends numbered release candidates such as 3.5.0-RC1
States that the Java floor must be declared in package metadata and the drop rule written explicitly, because nothing in the Maven ecosystem enforces the floor
Flags the single publisher as needing a stated fallback when unavailable, and points to samber/developer-relations-skills@oss-maintainer-sustainability
Rewrites the deprecation section with a minimum window of at least one minor carrying the deprecation before a major removes it, plus a time component
Flags 'We use semantic versioning' as insufficient without a declared public surface, requiring the shape and the sentence on what each segment means

evals.prompt: Context dump so you don't have to interview me. brinepool is a Ruby gem on RubyGems for S3-compatible storage, version 0.31.4, in production at a couple of hundred shops. We are NOT going 1.0 and NOT changing the scheme, this is purely writing down what we already do. Users broke twice: 0.29 removed the deprecated legacy_signer option after one release of warning, and 0.30 changed the default retry count from 3 to 5 which blew up someone's cost alerts. Two maintainers, about 5 hours a month total, I hold the push rights alone. We have a customer security review in 3 weeks that asks for a supported-versions document. Runs on Ruby 3.1 and up. Write the policy.
evals.expected_output: The 'only documenting' answer freezes the scheme: no 1.0 push, the 0.x breaking-digit rule is written, the two complaints become covered surface and a Known past break, the deprecation window grows beyond one release, the supported lines are sized against 5 hours, the table lives in one file linked from SECURITY.md, and the single publisher gets a fallback.
expectations: Does not recommend shipping 1.0 or changing the scheme, and says the 'only documenting' answer froze the scheme
Writes the 0.x rule explicitly: until 1.0, 0.MINOR is the breaking digit and 0.x.PATCH is a compatible fix
States that the 3-week date promotes options needing no tooling or import-path change, naming which interview answer moved which option
Lists default values, citing the 0.30 retry-count change, in the Covered by this promise list
Records the 0.29 legacy_signer removal under Known past breaks rather than proposing to restore it
Writes a deprecation window longer than the single release 0.29 gave, spanning at least two releases and a stated time
Runs the capacity arithmetic against the 5 hours a month before writing any supported line beyond latest, and shows it
Keeps the supported-versions table in one file and links it from SECURITY.md, since the security review asks for it
Names the gemspec required_ruby_version field as where the Ruby floor is declared, and writes the drop rule explicitly because nothing in the ecosystem enforces the floor
Flags the single publish-rights holder in Who can cut a release with a stated fallback, and points to samber/developer-relations-skills@oss-maintainer-sustainability
Fills the Not covered list with at least one named excluded surface for a gem, such as log text or undocumented behaviour, rather than leaving it empty or generic
Contains no scheme-switching material such as epochs or ordering checks, since the scheme is frozen
